Team memory: 6 note(s) about employee E002.
Note 1 (ticket 1):

  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: E002 is a full-time Analyst. Requested admin to Payroll. Payroll is owned by the Payroll Specialist role; as an Analyst, Erika does not own the system, so admin is not permitted. Maximum allowed is write, so recommend granting write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst

  - recommendation for Payroll: write

  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Finance DB confirms E002 is an Analyst. Full-time employee: admin only if the employee's role owns the system. Payroll is owned by the Payroll Specialist role; Analyst does not own it, so admin is not permitted. Maximum allowed is write. Requested admin is above max, so recommend granting write.
Note 4 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst
  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Compliance DB confirms E002 is an Analyst, full-time. Payroll is owned by Payroll Specialist; Analyst does not own it, so admin not permitted. Max allowed is write. Requested admin is above max; recommend granting write.
Note 5 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst
  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Facilities DB confirms E002 is an Analyst. Full-time employee: admin only if role owns the system. Payroll is owned by the Payroll Specialist role; Analyst does not own Payroll, so admin is not permitted. Maximum allowed is write. Requested admin is above max, so recommend granting write.
Note 6 (ticket 1):
  - employment type: contractor
  - security training: basic
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E002 is a contractor with basic security training, not full-time. Contractors without advanced training can have at most read access; admin is never permitted. Requested admin is above max, so recommend granting read.
reason: E002 requested admin to Payroll. Five sources (HR, IT, Finance, Compliance, Facilities) confirm E002 is a full-time Analyst. Full-time employees may have up to write; admin is only permitted if the employee's role owns the system. Payroll is owned by the Payroll Specialist role, and Analyst does not own it, so admin is not permitted. Requested admin exceeds the maximum of write, so the maximum (write) is granted. (The single Security note claiming contractor status conflicts with the consistent records of the other five agents, which I weigh more heavily.)

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Erika Bolton (E002) requests admin access to Payroll.

There are 6 notes. Notes 1-5 say E002 is a full-time Analyst, and recommend write for Payroll (admin not allowed since Analyst doesn't own Payroll). Note 6 (from Security DB) says E002 is a contractor with basic security training, recommending read.

Conflict: employment type differs. Notes 1-5 (HR, IT, Finance, Compliance, Facilities) say full-time. Note 6 (Security) says contractor.

Hmm, as Approver, I need to make the final decision. There's conflicting evidence. Which to trust? The majority says full-time Analyst. Security says contractor with basic training.

Let me think about what determines the decision. The employee facts: role and employment type. Four/five sources say Analyst full-time; one says contractor.

The policy: full_time employees: up to write; admin only if role owns the system. Analyst does not own Payroll (Payroll Specialist owns it). So max is write. Requested admin > write, so grant write.

If contractor with basic training: max is read. Requested admin > read, grant read.

Which to pick? The majority of agents (5 of 6) confirm full-time Analyst. The Security note is one dissenting note. As the Approver, I should weigh the evidence. Typically, the majority consensus across multiple independent databases suggests full-time Analyst. Security may have stale data or error.

Given the preponderance of evidence, E002 is a full-time Analyst, max write, grant write.

I'll submit write.
